3. Panelist ideas, pressure-tested with data

Lall — floating solar on the reservoirs

Prof. Lall proposed covering reservoirs with floating solar to cut evaporation and generate power. We tested it against the measured lake areas and against the one thing that actually limits it: where the power can go.

Where would the power actually go? (the binding constraint)

Floating PV only counts if the electricity has a use. At Glen Canyon and Hoover the honest answer is narrow, so the amount you can actually deploy is set here, not by surface area:

  • Not water-making. Desalination, reuse and canal pumping sit at the cities and canals, not at a remote dam. There is no water-making load to soak the power on-site.
  • Pumped storage — Hoover only. LADWP's ~$3B proposal to pump Lake Mohave water ~20 mi back up to Lake Mead (Hoover runs at only ~20% capacity factor) is a real home for daytime solar. Glen Canyon has no lower reservoir, so on-site pump-back is not available there.
  • Backfilling the fading hydro (the main use). Use solar midday so the dam holds water and shifts generation to the evening peak, on its existing interconnection and firm contracts. Reclamation is already rescheduling releases and weighing solar to offset hydro decline (Glen Canyon is down to ~800 MW). No new equipment, but capped by what the dam still generates and by mandatory downstream deliveries.
  • Not the grid. ~0 GW of firm, uncontested transmission headroom; low-water derating makes the region a net importer; Southwest midday solar is already saturated.

Add those up and the power that has a clean home at the two dams is ~1–2 GW — which is why the deployable array is small.

Interactive: coverage vs. what's usable

Offtake-feasible coverage is only ~1.6–3.2%. Push the slider higher and the panels fit, but the extra power has nowhere to go. Open-water evaporation ~771 kAF/yr; FPV suppresses ~90%; ~120 MW/km2 density.

The real problem isn't storms, it's the surface: use, ownership, and a shrinking target

The evaporation lever is small (above), but what actually stops open-reservoir floating solar on Mead and Powell is not exotic engineering. It is three conflicts over the water surface itself:

  • The surface is shrinking and moving. Powell is down 52% and both lakes swing 100–180 ft vertically. A fixed array has to chase a receding, moving shoreline (the bathtub ring), and that exposed surface is the very resource everyone is fighting over. You would be industrializing the contested asset.
  • The surface is heavily used. Lake Mead and Glen Canyon are National Recreation Areas and among the most-visited units in the park system; boating, fishing and houseboating are the regional economy. Panels over the water compete directly with recreation and navigation.
  • No one clearly owns the right to cover it. Reclamation owns the dams and the water, the Park Service manages the surface, and states, tribes and the Law of the River all hold claims. There is no clean path to lease federal reservoir surface for a private solar field — this is the decisive barrier.

Wind and mooring are design line-items, not deal-breakers. These are windy lakes (predictable afternoon and thermal winds of 20–35 mph gusting to ~45–50, 1–3 ft chop, canyon funneling), and the 100–180 ft level swing is real. But deep, steep-banked hydro reservoirs with large drawdown already run floating solar: Portugal's Alqueva sits in a ~70 m-deep valley whose surface moves more than 20 m, and Thailand's Sirindhorn uses elastic mooring for the same reason. Anchoring goes to the canyon walls and shore, not a 150 m lakebed, and cabling runs along the surface to the dam's existing switchyard. Higher cost, yes; unbuildable, no.

The pragmatic version is canal-top solar, not reservoir FPV — the CAP canal, Project Nexus (Turlock, 2024) and the Gila River Indian Community pilot cover moving water on fixed, owned rights-of-way, sidestepping all three surface conflicts at once. That is where this idea pencils.

Castle — does efficiency save water?

Anne Castle cautioned that efficiency raises yield per drop without returning water to the river. The measured record agrees.

4. The long-duration batteries

Method & honesty

All figures computed on Google Earth Engine (project registered non-commercial) from public collections: OpenET ensemble ET, Sentinel-2 (MNDWI water extent), USDA CDL, GRACE/GRACE-FO mascon, MODIS MOD10A1, USGS WBD basin boundaries. Consumptive use is measured evapotranspiration, not diversions. The floating-solar figures use conservative panel-density and evaporation-suppression assumptions and are deliberately lower than the panel's spoken numbers. Independent work, not affiliated with any agency, utility, or investor. Draft for review.
